Abstract:
<jats:p>The integration of flexible materials with optical sensing technologies has advanced wearable optical biosensors, offering significant potential in personalized medicine, health monitoring, and disease prevention. This review summarizes the recent advancements in flexible materials for wearable optical biosensors, with a focus on materials such as polymer substrates, nanostructured materials, MXenes, hydrogels, and textile-based integrated platforms. These materials enhance the functionality, sensitivity, and adaptability of sensors, particularly in wearable applications. The review also explores various optical sensing mechanisms, including surface plasmon resonance (SPR), optical fiber sensing, fluorescence sensing, chemiluminescence, and surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), emphasizing their role in improving the detection capabilities for biomarkers, physiological parameters, and environmental pollutants. Despite significant advancements, critical challenges remain in the fabrication and practical deployment of flexible optical biosensors, particularly regarding the long-term stability of materials under dynamic environments, maintaining reliable biocompatibility during prolonged skin contact, and minimizing signal interference caused by motion artifacts and environmental fluctuations. Addressing these issues is vital to ensure robustness and accuracy in real-world applications. Looking forward, future research should emphasize the development of multifunctional and miniaturized devices, the integration of wireless communication and intelligent data analytics, and the improvement of environmental resilience. Such innovations are expected to accelerate the transition of flexible optical biosensors from laboratory research to practical clinical and consumer healthcare applications, paving the way for intelligent health management and early disease diagnostics. Overall, flexible optical biosensors hold great promise in personalized health management, early disease diagnosis, and continuous physiological monitoring, with the potential to revolutionize the healthcare sector.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The biopharmaceutical industry must guarantee the efficiency and biosafety of biological medicines, which are quite sensitive to cell culture process variability. Real‐time monitoring procedures based on vibrational spectroscopy such as near‐infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, are then emerging to support innovative strategies for retro‐control of key parameters as substrates and by‐product concentration. Whereas monitoring models are mainly constructed using partial least squares regression (PLSR), spectroscopic models based on artificial neural networks (ANNR) and support vector regression (SVR) are emerging with promising results. Unfortunately, analysis of their performance in cell culture monitoring has been limited. This study was then focused to assess their performance and suitability for the cell culture process challenges. PLSR had inferior values of the determination coefficient (R2) for all the monitored parameters (i.e., 0.85, 0.93, and 0.98, respectively for the PLSR, SVR, and ANNR models for glucose). In general, PLSR had a limited performance while models based on ANNR and SVR have been shown superior due to better management of inter‐batch heterogeneity and enhanced specificity. Overall, the use of SVR and ANNR for the generation of calibration models enhanced the potential of NIR spectroscopy as a monitoring tool.

Abstract:
The analysis of infrared spectroscopy of substances is a non-invasive measurement technique that can be used in analytics. Although the main objective of this study is to provide a review of machine learning (ML) algorithms that have been reported for analyzing near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy from traditional machine learning methods to deep network architectures, we also provide different NIR measurement modes, instruments, signal preprocessing methods, etc. Firstly, four different measurement modes available in NIR are reviewed, different types of NIR instruments are compared, and a summary of NIR data analysis methods is provided. Secondly, the public NIR spectroscopy datasets are briefly discussed, with links provided. Thirdly, the widely used data preprocessing and feature selection algorithms that have been reported for NIR spectroscopy are presented. Then, the majority of the traditional machine learning methods and deep network architectures that are commonly employed are covered. Finally, we conclude that developing the integration of a variety of machine learning algorithms in an efficient and lightweight manner is a significant future research direction.

The excerpt frames PLSR (often called PLS) as a largely linear, lower-dimensional approach. It is widely accepted for NIR calibration and cell-culture monitoring because it is comparatively interpretable and fits regulatory lifecycle-management practices, but its predictive capacity can be limited when spectral relationships are nonlinear. ANN and SVR are presented as nonlinear alternatives with greater flexibility for modeling complex relationships. ANN uses supervised learning through weighted artificial neurons and biases to map spectra to concentrations. SVR maps inputs into a higher-dimensional feature space and fits a relatively flat regression function while constraining errors within an epsilon threshold; slack variables handle infeasible constraints. The cited literature generally reports ANNR and SVR as more predictive than PLSR for spectroscopic data, although this excerpt does not provide the study’s numerical performance results or establish which of ANN versus SVR was best. The study acquired 168 spectra from six CHO bioreactor cultures, using 135 samples for model calibration and 33 for validation. The calibration data were partitioned with the Kennard–Stone algorithm, and the validation set was withheld from calibration. Models predicted viable cell density, glucose, lactate, and glutamine from NIR spectra. A separate batch culture using ActiPro medium was also used as an independent test of prediction capability.

The main dataset contained 168 samples: 135 calibration samples used for model development and cross-validation, and 33 independent validation samples reserved for final performance assessment. Samples were partitioned with the Kennard–Stone algorithm, and the validation set was not used during calibration. PLSR latent-variable selection used venetian-windows cross-validation based on Q²Y. The same selected spectral preprocessing was applied across methods to make the regression comparison fair. SVR used an epsilon-regression formulation with a Gaussian radial-basis kernel, with gamma and epsilon optimized by venetian-windows cross-validation. ANNR architecture was screened for neuron number, and early stopping with tanh activation was used to limit overfitting. Models were selected using low RMSECV and RMSEP. Quantitative comparison was defined around accuracy (RMSEP), precision (mean residual and residual-variance tests), and linearity (calibration R² and Durbin–Watson analysis). Qualitative validation used repeated real-time spectra, including inter-batch heterogeneity, glucose-spiking specificity, internal validation, and an independent culture medium for external validation. However, these pages do not report the actual method-by-method performance differences; they only establish the design and validation framework. {"answer": "# State of the Art: In-Line Vibrational Spectroscopy Coupled to Automated/Flow Systems and Sensor Fusion for Electrolyte Composition Monitoring

## Overview

The coupling of vibrational spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR, Raman, NIR, UV-Vis) with automated liquid-handling or flow systems as real-time composition sensors has advanced substantially, driven by process analytical technology (PAT) frameworks and the emerging self-driving laboratory paradigm. Simultaneously, sensor fusion — the combination of spectroscopy with physical property measurements such as ionic conductivity on the same sample — has been demonstrated in several application domains. The following synthesizes the current literature across the four requested areas.

The table below summarizes the key studies discussed in this review.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## (a) Combined Spectroscopy + Conductivity Flow Cells for Electrolyte Speciation

The most mature demonstrations of spectroscopy–conductivity sensor fusion come from industrial process monitoring rather than battery electrolyte research per se. Bryan, Levitskaia, and Casella (2013) developed a fiber-coupled monitoring system for radiochemical reprocessing streams in which Raman spectroscopy and Vis-NIR absorbance probes were deployed remotely in flowing PUREX-process aqueous and organic streams, supplemented by conductivity, Coriolis density, temperature, and flow measurements (pqac-00000010). Raman was used primarily for concentrated Raman-active species (uranyl, oxo-anions, water, organics), while Vis-NIR absorption tracked actinides whose concentrations made Raman quantification impractical. Conductivity and density provided independent bulk-composition constraints, and PLS chemometric models trained on static spectra were validated with online centrifugal-contactor extraction tests.

In the CO₂-capture domain, Kachko et al. (Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2015, 54, 5769–5776; DOI: 10.1021/acs.iecr.5b00691) demonstrated a comprehensive multi-sensor chemometric system fusing NIR absorption spectroscopy with in-line conductivity, density, pH, sound velocity, and refractive index for real-time monitoring of aqueous amine solvents at a postcombustion CO₂-capture pilot plant (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020). A temperature-dependent PLS model was constructed with 53 designed compositions (fractional factorial, 5 levels) and predicted AMP, PZ, and CO₂ concentrations with average deviations of ±1.8%, ±1.3%, and ±3.9%, respectively, validated against offline LC-MS and hot-phosphoric-acid analysis over nearly 850 hours of pilot-plant operation (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000022). The NIR flow-through cell used a 5 mm path length with fiber-optic coupling and a tungsten-halogen source spanning 1017–2044 nm (pqac-00000020).

For dilute or moderately concentrated mixtures where components absorb independently, these methods are highly effective. Angulo et al. ## (a) Combined Spectroscopy + Conductivity Flow Cells for Electrolyte Speciation

The most mature demonstrations of spectroscopy–conductivity sensor fusion come from industrial process monitoring rather than battery electrolyte research per se. Bryan, Levitskaia, and Casella (2013) developed a fiber-coupled monitoring system for radiochemical reprocessing streams in which Raman spectroscopy and Vis-NIR absorbance probes were deployed remotely in flowing PUREX-process aqueous and organic streams, supplemented by conductivity, Coriolis density, temperature, and flow measurements (bryan2013spectroscopiconlinemonitoring pages 1-3). Raman was used primarily for concentrated Raman-active species (uranyl, oxo-anions, water, organics), while Vis-NIR absorption tracked actinides whose concentrations made Raman quantification impractical. Conductivity and density provided independent bulk-composition constraints, and PLS chemometric models trained on static spectra were validated with online centrifugal-contactor extraction tests.

In the CO₂-capture domain, Kachko et al. (Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2015, 54, 5769–5776; DOI: 10.1021/acs.iecr.5b00691) demonstrated a comprehensive multi-sensor chemometric system fusing NIR absorption spectroscopy with in-line conductivity, density, pH, sound velocity, and refractive index for real-time monitoring of aqueous amine solvents at a postcombustion CO₂-capture pilot plant (kachko2015realtimeprocessmonitoring pages 6-7, kachko2015realtimeprocessmonitoring pages 1-2, kachko2015realtimeprocessmonitoring pages 3-4). A temperature-dependent PLS model was constructed with 53 designed compositions (fractional factorial, 5 levels) and predicted AMP, PZ, and CO₂ concentrations with average deviations of ±1.8%, ±1.3%, and ±3.9%, respectively, validated against offline LC-MS and hot-phosphoric-acid analysis over nearly 850 hours of pilot-plant operation (kachko2015realtimeprocessmonitoring pages 6-7, kachko2015realtimeprocessmonitoring pages 7-8). The NIR flow-through cell used a 5 mm path length with fiber-optic coupling and a tungsten-halogen source spanning 1017–2044 nm (kachko2015realtimeprocessmonitoring pages 3-4).

While no single published study was identified that integrates exclusively an ATR-FTIR crystal and a conductivity electrode into a single monolithic flow cell specifically for battery electrolyte speciation, the architectural patterns above — spectroscopy plus conductivity plus other physical properties, all measured in series or in parallel on a flowing bypass stream — provide a proven blueprint. The Carrillo-Bohórquez, Kumar, and Kuroda perspective (J. Phys. Chem. C 2024, 128, 18695–18710; DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.4c06002) explicitly advocates coupling spectroscopy with transport measurements including conductivity as essential for characterizing high-concentration electrolytes, because spectroscopic signatures alone are ambiguous when extensive ion pairing and aggregation are present (carrillobohorquez2024thechallengeof pages 10-14, carrillobohorquez2024thechallengeof pages 30-33).

## (b) Chemometrics (PLS, MCR-ALS, CLS) vs. Neural Network / Nonlinear Models

### Linear approaches and their limitations

Classical least squares (CLS) and PLS regression assume an approximately linear relationship between absorbance and concentration (Beer–Lambert additivity). For dilute or moderately concentrated mixtures where components absorb independently, these methods are highly effective. Angulo et al. (Digital Discovery 2022, 1, 35–44; DOI: 10.1039/d1dd00027f) showed that for aqueous mixtures of up to six components measured by FTIR in a flow cell, simple linear regression (including PCR) achieved R² = 0.955–0.986 and MAE = 0.28–0.52 wt%, consistently outperforming a one-hidden-layer artificial neural network (ANN) with R² = 0.854–0.977 (angulo2022machinelearningenhanced pages 1-3, angulo2022machinelearningenhanced pages 8-9). However, these mixtures were prepared under approximately additive conditions, and the authors used Beer's law to generate synthetic training spectra (angulo2022machinelearningenhanced pages 3-4).

### MCR-ALS and blind source separation

Maggioni, Kocevska, and Rousseau (2019) applied an MCR-ALS blind source separation workflow (SVD rank estimation → ICA initialization → constrained MCR-ALS with non-negativity and mass-balance closure) to simultaneous Raman and ATR-FTIR spectra of a five-sodium-salt aqueous simulant (maggioni2019blindsourceseparation pages 1-2, maggioni2019blindsourceseparation pages 2-3). IR source/reference correlations exceeded 0.95, but residuals near nitrate/nitrite bands revealed deviations attributed to nonlinear nitrate–nitrite interactions, producing misleading components — direct evidence that Beer–Lambert superposition breaks down even in relatively simple multicomponent ionic solutions (maggioni2019blindsourceseparation pages 2-3). The authors concluded that MCR-ALS works well under linear conditions but generates spurious spectral components when nonadditivity is present.

### Nonlinear approaches: ANN, SVR, and quadratic PLS

When Beer–Lambert additivity fails — as in concentrated electrolytes where ion pairing, aggregation, and solvent-restructuring change spectral shapes nonlinearly with concentration — nonlinear models are needed. Zavala-Ortiz et al. (Biotechnol. Bioeng. 2022, 119, 535–549; DOI: 10.1002/bit.27997) conducted a rigorous three-way comparison of PLS, ANN regression (ANNR), and support-vector regression (SVR) for in-situ NIR monitoring under nonlinear conditions. For glucose, R² values were 0.85, 0.93, and 0.98 and RMSEP was 3.37, 2.29, and 1.32 mM for PLSR, SVR, and ANNR, respectively (zavala‐ortiz2022comparisonofpartial pages 25-29, zavala‐ortiz2022comparisonofpartial pages 12-15, zavala‐ortiz2022comparisonofpartial pages 1-5). SVR was the most precise overall, while ANNR generalized best across culture-medium changes (zavala‐ortiz2022comparisonofpartial pages 18-22, zavala‐ortiz2022comparisonofpartial pages 15-18).

Blanco et al. (Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst. 2000, 50, 75–82; DOI: 10.1016/s0169-7439(99)00048-9) showed that for intrinsically nonlinear NIR systems, quadratic PLS variants and PC-ANN produced comparable results, with PC-ANN slightly superior but requiring more optimization effort. Critically, they found that scatter correction (SNV) could linearize scattering-induced nonlinearity sufficiently for standard PLS, but intrinsic absorption-concentration nonlinearity required genuinely nonlinear methods (blanco2000nircalibrationin pages 1-2).

### Relevance to concentrated electrolytes

The Carrillo-Bohórquez et al. (2024) perspective establishes that high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs) present particular challenges: overlapping free-solvent, coordinated-solvent, contact-ion-pair, and aggregate spectral signatures; very short IR path lengths required by high absorption; ambiguous Raman band assignments where identical spectral signatures arise from chemically distinct species; and spectral responses that are non-additive because increasing salt concentration lowers the dielectric constant, strengthens electrostatic interactions, and drives extensive ion association (carrillobohorquez2024thechallengeof pages 10-14, yu2021beyondlocalsolvation pages 1-2, carrillobohorquez2024thechallengeof pages 6-10, carrillobohorquez2024thechallengeof pages 22-26). The perspective recommends combining spectroscopy with molecular dynamics simulation for interpretation and highlights high-throughput Raman as a promising avenue for rapid screening of compositional spaces (carrillobohorquez2024thechallengeof pages 22-26, carrillobohorquez2024thechallengeof pages 18-22).

## (c) Training Data Requirements and Validation Strategies

Training data requirements vary significantly with model complexity and mixture dimensionality:

- **Linear regression/PCR for FTIR (Angulo et al., 2022):** Performance for ternary aqueous mixtures saturated at approximately 40 training spectra; PCA–LR was nearly insensitive to training size above ≈25 spectra. ANN required substantially more training spectra and exhibited greater variability with training-set size (angulo2022machinelearningenhanced pages 8-9, angulo2022machinelearningenhanced pages 5-6). Experimental data used an 80/20 random train/test split repeated 200 times, and simulated spectra provided unlimited augmentation under the Beer–Lambert assumption (angulo2022machinelearningenhanced pages 9-10).

- **Multi-sensor PLS for CO₂ capture (Kachko et al., 2015):** A 5^(3−1) fractional factorial design generated 53 compositions (12 excluded for precipitation), with approximately 27 training and 26 testing compositions measured at three temperatures (25, 35, 40 °C) (kachko2016inlinemonitoringof pages 24-28, kachko2015realtimeprocessmonitoring pages 2-3). Latent-variable selection used leave-one-out cross-validation based on RMSEP (kachko2015realtimeprocessmonitoring pages 3-4). Final validation used offline analytical methods at the pilot plant.

- **ANN/SVR for in-situ NIR (Zavala-Ortiz et al., 2022):** 168 spectra from six bioreactor cultures were split 135/33 using the Kennard–Stone algorithm for calibration/validation. Venetian-windows cross-validation selected PLS latent variables and SVR hyperparameters, and ANN used early stopping to limit overfitting. An independent culture medium served as an external blind test (zavala‐ortiz2022comparisonofpartial pages 5-9, zavala‐ortiz2022comparisonofpartial pages 9-12).

- **MCR-ALS blind source separation (Maggioni et al., 2019):** Required only 17 samples (14 mixtures + 3 water blanks), but this is a self-modeling technique estimating the number of sources from SVD rank rather than training a regression model. Validation was performed by matching recovered spectra to a pure-component reference library (maggioni2019blindsourceseparation pages 1-2, maggioni2019blindsourceseparation pages 2-3).

A general trend emerges: linear models (CLS, PLS, PCR) require modest training sets (25–50 samples for 3–6 components), while nonlinear models (ANN, SVR) demand more data and careful regularization to avoid overfitting, but deliver superior performance when Beer–Lambert additivity fails.

## (d) Raman vs. IR Practicality for Fiber-Coupled Robotic Integration

Raman spectroscopy holds substantial practical advantages for integration into robotic and automated flow platforms:

1. **Minimal water interference:** Water has low polarizability and produces relatively weak Raman scattering, enabling direct measurements in aqueous electrolytes through glass or quartz, particularly in the biochemical/chemical fingerprint region of ~500–1800 cm⁻¹ (jurina2023applicationofspectroscopy pages 9-11, klaverdijk2025rapidcalibrationof pages 22-26). In contrast, mid-IR spectroscopy is severely hampered by strong water absorption, requiring ATR configurations with very short (~μm) effective path lengths.

2. **Fiber-optic compatibility:** Raman uses visible or near-IR excitation wavelengths (typically 532, 633, or 785 nm) that transmit efficiently through standard silica optical fibers, enabling remote probe heads connected by fiber cables of arbitrary length. This is well established in nuclear reprocessing, where fiber-coupled Raman probes are deployed in shielded hot cells (bryan2013spectroscopiconlinemonitoring pages 1-3). Autoclavable immersion probes and flow-cell assemblies for Raman are commercially available for bioprocessing (klaverdijk2025rapidcalibrationof pages 22-26).

3. **Demonstrated microfluidic and robotic integration:** Nelson et al. (Anal. Chem. 2021, 93, 1643–1651; DOI: 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c04225) combined micro-Raman with micro-UV-Vis absorbance for online monitoring of microfluidic liquid-liquid extraction flows, using quartz chips to minimize spectral interference (nelson2021enablingmicroscaleprocessing pages 5-6, nelson2021enablingmicroscaleprocessing pages 1-3). Seifrid et al. (Acc. Chem. Res. 2022, 55, 2454–2466; DOI: 10.1021/acs.accounts.2c00220) described self-driving laboratories using fiber-coupled UV-Vis absorbance and photoluminescence flow cells with robotic sample transfer orchestrated by ChemOS (seifrid2022autonomouschemicalexperiments pages 6-8).

4. **Mid-IR limitations for robotic integration:** ATR-FTIR requires intimate contact between the sample and an internal reflection element (typically diamond, ZnSe, or Ge), which constrains flow-cell geometry and makes remote fiber coupling difficult. Mid-IR fibers (chalcogenide, silver halide) exist but are fragile, expensive, and have limited transmission windows compared to silica fibers for Raman. The shallow ATR penetration depth is advantageous for highly absorbing aqueous samples but limits sensitivity for dilute analytes (jurina2023applicationofspectroscopy pages 18-20).

5. **Raman weaknesses:** Intrinsically weak Raman scattering cross-sections can be overwhelmed by fluorescence from impurities or colored solutions, and sensitivity for some ionic species (e.g., phosphate) may be inadequate (maggioni2019blindsourceseparation pages 1-2, klaverdijk2025rapidcalibrationof pages 22-26). The complementarity of Raman and ATR-FTIR is well illustrated by Maggioni et al. (2019), where phosphate was strongly IR-active but weakly Raman-active (maggioni2019blindsourceseparation pages 1-2).

6. **Miniaturization and portability:** Ilchenko et al. (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-47044-7) demonstrated centimeter-scale miniaturized Raman spectrometers with performance comparable to research-grade systems, suggesting that compact Raman modules are increasingly feasible for integration into robotic platforms.

## Summary and Outlook

The current state of the art demonstrates that vibrational spectroscopy can serve as a real-time composition sensor in automated and flow systems, and that fusing spectroscopy with physical properties like conductivity provides complementary constraints essential for resolving complex electrolyte compositions. However, a significant gap exists: no published study has yet demonstrated a purpose-built ATR-FTIR + conductivity flow cell specifically optimized for real-time speciation of concentrated multicomponent battery electrolytes with ion-pairing nonlinearity, together with a nonlinear chemometric model trained and blind-validated for that system. The closest existing work combines sensor fusion in simpler systems (CO₂-capture amines, nuclear waste simulants) or addresses the spectroscopic challenges of high-concentration electrolytes at a fundamental characterization level without real-time closed-loop implementation. Raman spectroscopy, with its superior fiber-coupling and water tolerance, appears to be the most practical modality for near-term robotic integration, while ATR-FTIR offers superior sensitivity and species coverage for many ionic analytes but at the cost of more constrained optical interfacing.

C 2024, 128, 18695–18710; DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.4c06002) explicitly advocates coupling spectroscopy with transport measurements including conductivity as essential for characterizing high-concentration electrolytes, because spectroscopic signatures alone are ambiguous when extensive ion pairing and aggregation are present (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000029).

## (b) Chemometrics (PLS, MCR-ALS, CLS) vs. Neural Network / Nonlinear Models

### Linear approaches and their limitations

Classical least squares (CLS) and PLS regression assume an approximately linear relationship between absorbance and concentration (Beer–Lambert additivity). For dilute or moderately concentrated mixtures where components absorb independently, these methods are highly effective. Angulo et al. (Digital Discovery 2022, 1, 35–44; DOI: 10.1039/d1dd00027f) showed that for aqueous mixtures of up to six components measured by FTIR in a flow cell, simple linear regression (including PCR) achieved R² = 0.955–0.986 and MAE = 0.28–0.52 wt%, consistently outperforming a one-hidden-layer artificial neural network (ANN) with R² = 0.854–0.977 (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). However, these mixtures were prepared under approximately additive conditions, and the authors used Beer's law to generate synthetic training spectra (pqac-00000002).

### MCR-ALS and blind source separation

Maggioni, Kocevska, and Rousseau (2019) applied an MCR-ALS blind source separation workflow (SVD rank estimation → ICA initialization → constrained MCR-ALS with non-negativity and mass-balance closure) to simultaneous Raman and ATR-FTIR spectra of a five-sodium-salt aqueous simulant (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000014). IR source/reference correlations exceeded 0.95, but residuals near nitrate/nitrite bands revealed deviations attributed to nonlinear nitrate–nitrite interactions, producing misleading components — direct evidence that Beer–Lambert superposition breaks down even in relatively simple multicomponent ionic solutions (pqac-00000026). The authors concluded that MCR-ALS works well under linear conditions but generates spurious spectral components when nonadditivity is present.

### Nonlinear approaches: ANN, SVR, and quadratic PLS

When Beer–Lambert additivity fails — as in concentrated electrolytes where ion pairing, aggregation, and solvent-restructuring change spectral shapes nonlinearly with concentration — nonlinear models are needed. Zavala-Ortiz et al. (Biotechnol. Bioeng. 2022, 119, 535–549; DOI: 10.1002/bit.27997) conducted a rigorous three-way comparison of PLS, ANN regression (ANNR), and support-vector regression (SVR) for in-situ NIR monitoring under nonlinear conditions. For glucose, R² values were 0.85, 0.93, and 0.98 and RMSEP was 3.37, 2.29, and 1.32 mM for PLSR, SVR, and ANNR, respectively (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). SVR was the most precise overall, while ANNR generalized best across culture-medium changes (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039).

Blanco et al. (Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst. 2000, 50, 75–82; DOI: 10.1016/s0169-7439(99)00048-9) showed that for intrinsically nonlinear NIR systems, quadratic PLS variants and PC-ANN produced comparable results, with PC-ANN slightly superior but requiring more optimization effort. Critically, they found that scatter correction (SNV) could linearize scattering-induced nonlinearity sufficiently for standard PLS, but intrinsic absorption-concentration nonlinearity required genuinely nonlinear methods (pqac-00000040).

### Relevance to concentrated electrolytes

The Carrillo-Bohórquez et al. (2024) perspective establishes that high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs) present particular challenges: overlapping free-solvent, coordinated-solvent, contact-ion-pair, and aggregate spectral signatures; very short IR path lengths required by high absorption; ambiguous Raman band assignments where identical spectral signatures arise from chemically distinct species; and spectral responses that are non-additive because increasing salt concentration lowers the dielectric constant, strengthens electrostatic interactions, and drives extensive ion association (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). The perspective recommends combining spectroscopy with molecular dynamics simulation for interpretation and highlights high-throughput Raman as a promising avenue for rapid screening of compositional spaces (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

## (c) Training Data Requirements and Validation Strategies

Training data requirements vary significantly with model complexity and mixture dimensionality:

- **Linear regression/PCR for FTIR (Angulo et al., 2022):** Performance for ternary aqueous mixtures saturated at approximately 40 training spectra; PCA–LR was nearly insensitive to training size above ≈25 spectra. ANN required substantially more training spectra and exhibited greater variability with training-set size (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). Experimental data used an 80/20 random train/test split repeated 200 times, and simulated spectra provided unlimited augmentation under the Beer–Lambert assumption (pqac-00000004).

- **Multi-sensor PLS for CO₂ capture (Kachko et al., 2015):** A 5^(3−1) fractional factorial design generated 53 compositions (12 excluded for precipitation), with approximately 27 training and 26 testing compositions measured at three temperatures (25, 35, 40 °C) (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019). Latent-variable selection used leave-one-out cross-validation based on RMSEP (pqac-00000020). Final validation used offline analytical methods at the pilot plant.

- **ANN/SVR for in-situ NIR (Zavala-Ortiz et al., 2022):** 168 spectra from six bioreactor cultures were split 135/33 using the Kennard–Stone algorithm for calibration/validation. Venetian-windows cross-validation selected PLS latent variables and SVR hyperparameters, and ANN used early stopping to limit overfitting. An independent culture medium served as an external blind test (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035).

- **MCR-ALS blind source separation (Maggioni et al., 2019):** Required only 17 samples (14 mixtures + 3 water blanks), but this is a self-modeling technique estimating the number of sources from SVD rank rather than training a regression model. Validation was performed by matching recovered spectra to a pure-component reference library (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000014).

A general trend emerges: linear models (CLS, PLS, PCR) require modest training sets (25–50 samples for 3–6 components), while nonlinear models (ANN, SVR) demand more data and careful regularization to avoid overfitting, but deliver superior performance when Beer–Lambert additivity fails.

## (d) Raman vs. IR Practicality for Fiber-Coupled Robotic Integration

Raman spectroscopy holds substantial practical advantages for integration into robotic and automated flow platforms:

1. **Minimal water interference:** Water has low polarizability and produces relatively weak Raman scattering, enabling direct measurements in aqueous electrolytes through glass or quartz, particularly in the biochemical/chemical fingerprint region of ~500–1800 cm⁻¹ (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000015). In contrast, mid-IR spectroscopy is severely hampered by strong water absorption, requiring ATR configurations with very short (~μm) effective path lengths.

2. **Fiber-optic compatibility:** Raman uses visible or near-IR excitation wavelengths (typically 532, 633, or 785 nm) that transmit efficiently through standard silica optical fibers, enabling remote probe heads connected by fiber cables of arbitrary length. This is well established in nuclear reprocessing, where fiber-coupled Raman probes are deployed in shielded hot cells (pqac-00000010). Autoclavable immersion probes and flow-cell assemblies for Raman are commercially available for bioprocessing (pqac-00000015).

3. **Demonstrated microfluidic and robotic integration:** Nelson et al. (Anal. Chem. 2021, 93, 1643–1651; DOI: 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c04225) combined micro-Raman with micro-UV-Vis absorbance for online monitoring of microfluidic liquid-liquid extraction flows, using quartz chips to minimize spectral interference (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012). Seifrid et al. (Acc. Chem. Res. 2022, 55, 2454–2466; DOI: 10.1021/acs.accounts.2c00220) described self-driving laboratories using fiber-coupled UV-Vis absorbance and photoluminescence flow cells with robotic sample transfer orchestrated by ChemOS (pqac-00000032).

4. **Mid-IR limitations for robotic integration:** ATR-FTIR requires intimate contact between the sample and an internal reflection element (typically diamond, ZnSe, or Ge), which constrains flow-cell geometry and makes remote fiber coupling difficult. Mid-IR fibers (chalcogenide, silver halide) exist but are fragile, expensive, and have limited transmission windows compared to silica fibers for Raman. The shallow ATR penetration depth is advantageous for highly absorbing aqueous samples but limits sensitivity for dilute analytes (pqac-00000013).

5. **Raman weaknesses:** Intrinsically weak Raman scattering cross-sections can be overwhelmed by fluorescence from impurities or colored solutions, and sensitivity for some ionic species (e.g., phosphate) may be inadequate (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000015). The complementarity of Raman and ATR-FTIR is well illustrated by Maggioni et al. (2019), where phosphate was strongly IR-active but weakly Raman-active (pqac-00000008).

6. **Miniaturization and portability:** Ilchenko et al. (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-47044-7) demonstrated centimeter-scale miniaturized Raman spectrometers with performance comparable to research-grade systems, suggesting that compact Raman modules are increasingly feasible for integration into robotic platforms.

## Summary and Outlook

The current state of the art demonstrates that vibrational spectroscopy can serve as a real-time composition sensor in automated and flow systems, and that fusing spectroscopy with physical properties like conductivity provides complementary constraints essential for resolving complex electrolyte compositions. However, a significant gap exists: no published study has yet demonstrated a purpose-built ATR-FTIR + conductivity flow cell specifically optimized for real-time speciation of concentrated multicomponent battery electrolytes with ion-pairing nonlinearity, together with a nonlinear chemometric model trained and blind-validated for that system. The closest existing work combines sensor fusion in simpler systems (CO₂-capture amines, nuclear waste simulants) or addresses the spectroscopic challenges of high-concentration electrolytes at a fundamental characterization level without real-time closed-loop implementation. Raman spectroscopy, with its superior fiber-coupling and water tolerance, appears to be the most practical modality for near-term robotic integration, while ATR-FTIR offers superior sensitivity and species coverage for many ionic analytes but at the cost of more constrained optical interfacing.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes multitarget regression machine-learning models applied to FTIR absorption spectra for simultaneous concentration prediction in multicomponent mixtures. It reports simulated FTIR spectra for mixtures containing up to six components in water, with seven machine-learning algorithms tested. Across the simulated-data models, mean absolute errors ranged from 0 to 0.27 wt%. The methodology was also validated using experimental data from mixtures prepared with programmable pumps and an FTIR transmission flow cell. Experimental tests involved mixtures of up to four chemically similar components, specifically alcohols (glycerol, isopropanol, and 1-butanol) and nitriles (acrylonitrile, adiponitrile, and propionitrile). Linear regression produced R² values of 0.955–0.986, while artificial neural networks produced R² values of 0.854–0.977; the corresponding MAEs were 0.28–0.52 wt% for component concentrations of 4–10 wt%. The provided pages do not mention ATR-FTIR or Raman spectra, comparisons with partial least squares (PLS) or classical least squares, the specific neural-network architecture, or the number of training spectra/samples. They establish mixture size and concentration ranges but do not provide the training-data quantity needed for a direct comparison.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes machine-learning models for quantitative prediction of multicomponent chemical compositions from FTIR spectra. The evaluated implementations included linear regression (LR), multilayer perceptron regression/artificial neural networks (ANN), decision-tree regression, random-forest regression, support-vector regression, ridge regression with cross-validation, and k-nearest-neighbors regression. Simulated mixture spectra were generated using Beer’s law, with concentration matrices constructed for training and test sets; the models predicted component concentrations from the resulting spectra. For practical model mixtures, LR and ANN achieved R² values of approximately 0.98–0.99 and 0.94–0.98, respectively. LR was simpler, less computationally expensive, and consistently more accurate than ANN in the reported experiments, making it the preferred approach for quantitative composition prediction. Training-data analysis for ternary aqueous mixtures found that performance increased rapidly with the number of spectra and then saturated at roughly 40 training spectra. ANN required more training spectra and was more sensitive to training-set size than LR. The excerpt does not provide details or comparisons involving partial least squares (PLS) or classical least squares (CLS), and it specifically discusses FTIR rather than Raman spectra.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a supervised, multitarget machine-learning approach for predicting the concentrations of all components in multicomponent FTIR mixtures from absorbance values at multiple wavenumbers. The authors generated synthetic training spectra by linearly combining pure-component spectra, with molar fractions as weights, and then validated the models against experimentally measured mixture spectra. The model system included up to six aqueous components—acrylonitrile, adiponitrile, propionitrile, EDTA, phosphate ions, and tetramethylammonium ions—with overlapping or similar absorption features. Several algorithms were evaluated, and the strongest reported performance came from artificial neural networks (ANNs) and linear regression preceded by principal component analysis (PCA), i.e., principal component regression (PCR). Across the tested numbers and identities of components, these methods achieved R² values of 0.854–0.986 and mean absolute errors of 0.28–0.52 wt%. The excerpt contrasts this approach conceptually with conventional FTIR analysis, which often uses only selected absorption peaks or manually selected spectral regions, whereas the ML method uses spectral correlations across the data. It does not report a comparison with ordinary PLS or classical least squares, does not mention Raman or ATR-specific measurements, and does not state the number of training spectra or samples required. Earlier cited studies used SVMs and linear regression, but their training-data sizes and preprocessing details are only partly given here.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not describe machine-learning or neural-network models applied to ATR-FTIR or Raman spectra, and it provides no comparison with PLS regression or classical least squares. Instead, it presents a calibration-avoiding blind source separation (BSS) workflow. First, singular-value decomposition (SVD) is used to estimate the effective rank of the data matrix, interpreted as the number of detectable species. Second, independent component analysis (ICA) initializes multivariate curve resolution with alternating least squares (MCR-ALS); the MCR-ALS solution is constrained by physical requirements including non-negativity and mass-balance closure. Third, the recovered component spectra are matched against a pure-component reference library, allowing species identification and relative composition estimates through one-point calibration. Spectral preprocessing is applied to address baseline drift, spikes, and noise. The study used a simulant containing five sodium salts and measured both Raman and ATR-FTIR spectra. Measurements were collected for 17 samples: 14 with different compositions and 3 pure-water samples. The excerpt therefore indicates a small experimental dataset for BSS, not neural-network training. It reports that IR source identifications correlated above 0.95 with reference spectra, while Raman missed phosphate and produced two nitrate-related sources; Raman mole-fraction estimates nevertheless remained close to actual values.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a three-step blind source separation procedure applied to simultaneously collected Raman and ATR-FTIR spectra from a simulant mixture containing five ionic species in water. It is not a description of neural-network or conventional supervised machine-learning models. The number of latent species/components was selected by inspecting singular values, with six components retained for both Raman and IR; using more than six prevented reconstruction of the original dataset. Concentration information was estimated through a one-point calibration approach, rather than through a reported PLS, classical least-squares, or neural-network model. The dataset comprised only 17 samples: 14 with different compositions and three pure-water samples. The authors report that the approach worked effectively for IR when concentration linearity and linear spectral superposition held. For Raman, noise and mild nonlinearities limited performance: phosphate was obscured because its local signal-to-noise ratio was about 10 dB, and nitrate/nitrite interactions suggested a violation of Beer–Lambert linearity. The method nevertheless identified the main species and produced molar-fraction estimates close to actual values under noisy, mildly nonlinear conditions. No training-set size requirements, neural-network architecture, or quantitative comparison with PLS or classical least squares are provided in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general chemometric context but does not report specific machine-learning or neural-network models applied to ATR-FTIR or Raman spectra of multicomponent mixtures, nor does it give the amount of training data required. It states that spectroscopic quantification relates spectra or selected wavelengths to chemical properties using a calibration/training set for which spectra and reference measurements are available. Classical multiple linear regression (MLR) is described as straightforward, but multicollinearity can cause poor prediction and make standard MLR unsuitable. Principal component regression (PCR) addresses multicollinearity but may retain directions of maximum spectral variance that are not relevant to prediction. PLS is presented as the most widely used chemometric calibration method; it extracts latent variables that explain spectral variance while maximizing covariance with the responses. The excerpt warns that PCR and PLS require selection of the number of latent variables, since too few can underfit and too many can overfit. Cross-validation is recommended to select the number minimizing validation error. For nonlinear relationships, artificial neural networks (ANNs) are identified as self-adaptive, massively parallel machine-learning systems capable of learning cause-effect relationships through training. However, no ANN architecture, performance comparison against PLS or classical least squares, spectral modality-specific application, concentration ranges, or training-set size is included.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes machine-learning concentration prediction from FTIR absorbance spectra for multicomponent mixtures. Two model families were evaluated: linear regression (LR), with and without principal component analysis (PCA), and an artificial neural network (ANN). For the ANN, the reported configuration used one hidden layer with 12 neurons, a ReLU activation function, and a batch size of 60. PCA did not noticeably change ANN performance, but reduced its computational time by a factor of 10. In noise tests, LR generally outperformed ANN, with a mean absolute error (MAE) smaller by a factor of 5–10; with PCA, LR maintained relatively low errors below approximately 0.15 wt%, whereas ANN errors remained below about 0.8 wt% under the stated conditions. Training-size experiments indicated that LR without PCA stabilized at about 50 training spectra, while LR with PCA was nearly insensitive to training size once at least 25 spectra were used. ANN showed no clear trend with training-set size and greater variability. The experimental implementation used programmable pumps and a transmission FTIR flow cell, collecting 50 labeled spectra per day; absorbances at each wavenumber were predictors and mass concentrations were targets. The excerpt does not discuss ATR-FTIR or Raman spectra, nor does it provide comparisons with PLS or classical least-squares methods.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes UV-Vis and UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy as online tools for continuously operated microreactors, particularly for tracking liquid-phase concentrations, segmented-flow characteristics, nanoparticle synthesis, and changing nanoparticle geometries. UV-Vis measurements can provide very high temporal resolution (reported as 2 ms), while online integration supports live process quality control. UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy is also presented as compatible with fast, reproducible microfluidic synthesis and advanced chemometric analysis. Raman spectroscopy is introduced as a real-time chemical-fingerprinting method using monochromatic, commonly visible, light. It permits direct in-situ, online analyte detection when the flow system uses glass or quartz, which is relevant to fiber- or probe-coupled flow devices and potentially robotic platforms. However, this excerpt does not explicitly explain how Raman and UV-Vis-NIR measurements are combined in one monitoring system, nor does it compare Raman and IR specifically for fiber-coupled integration or robotic deployment. It does describe a complementary Raman/ATR-FTIR strategy for multicomponent salt solutions. Raman and IR measurements are collected simultaneously, and because the techniques have different activity and sensitivity patterns, combining them improves detection; for example, phosphate is weakly Raman-active but strongly IR-active. Their independence also allows mutual cross-validation of species identification and composition estimates. For blind source separation, the workflow first estimates the number of measurable species from the effective rank of the data matrix using singular values. It then uses ICA to initialize MCR-ALS. MCR-ALS is constrained by physical requirements including non-negativity and mass-balance closure, after preprocessing to reduce baseline drift, spikes, and noise. Finally, recovered spectra are compared with a pure-component reference library to identify species and estimate mole fractions using one-point calibration. In the reported five-sodium-salt simulant, IR performed better overall: identified sources had correlations above 0.95 with reference spectra. Raman did not identify phosphate and produced two nitrate-correlated sources, although its estimated mole fractions remained close to actual values.

Measurements were performed at constant temperature in a stirred 250-mL vessel, using 17 samples comprising 14 different compositions and three pure-water samples. A three-step blind source-separation procedure was applied to identify species and estimate their relative concentrations using a one-point calibration approach. Singular-value inspection indicated six components for both Raman and IR data. For Raman, residual analysis showed errors around the phosphate band near 880 cm−1 and the nitrate/carbonate region near 1649–1669 cm−1. Phosphate was not recovered because its local signal-to-noise ratio was only about 10 dB, despite an average Raman SNR of approximately 40 dB. Nitrate-related deviations suggested a violation of Beer–Lambert linearity, attributed to nonlinear interaction between nitrate and nitrite. The study concludes that the method works effectively for IR when concentration linearity and spectral superposition hold, while under noise and mild nonlinearities it can still identify the principal species and produce molar-fraction estimates close to actual values. No specific Raman-versus-IR fiber or platform advantages are stated.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a complementary online-monitoring strategy in which UV–vis absorbance and Raman spectroscopy measure different components of a flowing liquid–liquid extraction process. UV–vis tracks Nd3+ concentrations in the aqueous and organic phases through characteristic absorbance bands near 520, 580, 740, and 800 nm. Raman tracks nitrate and identifies organic-phase species; the aqueous phase has a prominent nitrate band near 1050 cm−1, whereas the organic phase exhibits C–H-related peaks and little nitrate signal at that wavelength. Separate partial least-squares (PLS) chemometric models were developed for nitrate from Raman spectra and neodymium from UV–vis spectra. Raman preprocessing included normalization for laser/electronics drift and first-derivative baseline correction; Nd modeling used Savitzky–Golay smoothing and derivative preprocessing. A combined model using aqueous and organic static spectra was applied to flowing measurements and showed good predictive performance. The excerpt also indicates that quartz minimizes spectral interference, but PMMA chips can be used with suitable background subtraction, supporting lower-cost microscale integration. snippets: A solvent blend of aqueous 2-amino-2-methyl-1-propanol (AMP) activated by piperazine (PZ) and loaded with CO2 was studied in a laboratory and also monitored at an industrial pilot plant.
The following solvent properties were measured: density (ρ), conductivity (Ω−1), pH, sound velocity (SV), refractive index (nD), and near-infrared (NIR) absorption.
A model based on the partial least-squares (PLS) regression algorithm was used for prediction of the concentrations from the set of measured data.
The temperature dependency was included in the model by using the calibration data set of the measurements conducted at three temperatures: 25, 35, 40 °C.
The conﬁrmation of the applicability of the method via testing at an industrial pilot plant with subsequent validation is presented as well.
During the measurement campaign at the pilot plant, the whole set of samples was used as a calibration database for the PLS model.
The ﬁnal calibration set of samples was subjected to analysis using measurements of six variables: density (ρ), conductivity (Ω−1), pH, sound velocity (SV), refractive index (nD), and NIR absorbance.

Calibration samples were used to establish correlations between known mixture compositions and measured physical and spectroscopic responses. Separate PLS-1 models were built for each chemical component using either the physical measurements, NIR signals, or the complete measurement set. The independent-variable matrix contained the controllable chemical concentrations, while the response data included five physical properties and NIR measurements. Models were constructed in MATLAB using PLSREGRESS, with latent variables linking concentrations to measured responses. Performance was assessed using RMSEP. Leave-one-out cross-validation examined the influence of latent-variable number, and the simpler model was retained when adding another latent variable reduced RMSEP by no more than 2%. Temperature dependence was incorporated by training the model with measurements collected at different temperatures, rather than updating the model through polynomial interpolation. NIR preprocessing included conversion to absorbance, spectral windowing, Savitzky-Golay smoothing, derivative evaluation, selection of the first derivative, and mean-centering.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies NMR, IR, Raman, time-resolved laser spectroscopy, X-ray scattering, neutron scattering, and dielectric spectroscopy as approaches for molecular-level characterization of high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs). NMR can probe nearly all electrolyte constituents, including solvent, cation, and anion, but its sub-nanosecond time-resolution limit is poorly matched to the picosecond-to-nanosecond dynamics of concentrated electrolytes. Consequently, spectroscopic speciation and structural interpretation commonly rely on averaged spectral signatures and theoretical or molecular-modeling approaches rather than direct resolution of all molecular environments. Electrophoretic NMR provides additional transport-related information, but also requires modeling to connect observed properties with molecular mechanisms. Concentration-dependent ion association is an important complication: HCEs exhibit ion aggregation, while localized HCEs can preserve solvation structures but alter ionic aggregation and conduction mechanisms. The excerpt does not specifically detail nonlinear spectroscopic effects or provide a dedicated treatment of how ion pairing changes spectral line shapes or intensities. It does, however, indicate that overlapping contributions from multiple species and changing aggregation states make molecular interpretation model-dependent. Related scattering methods likewise require deconvolution and are not uniquely interpretable, reinforcing the need to combine spectroscopy with simulations and complementary measurements.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes spectroscopy of high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs) as difficult because concentrated samples contain many chemically distinct species whose spectral features overlap or are not uniquely assigned. Neutron scattering provides structural and dynamical information and can exploit isotope substitution to simplify separation of elemental contributions, but it requires specialized facilities and expensive isotope-edited samples. FTIR is useful for probing vibrational modes sensitive to local chemical environments, including solvation shells, ionic speciation, and cation coordination numbers. However, some common HCE components lack localized infrared probes, and high salt/solvent concentrations impose very short optical path lengths. Ultrafast pump-probe and two-dimensional IR methods access molecular dynamics, including ion-pair formation and dissociation on approximately hundred-picosecond timescales, although interpreting such nonlinear/time-resolved measurements generally depends on prior molecular knowledge and modeling. Raman spectroscopy can distinguish free versus coordinated solvent and identify contact ion pairs and aggregates, but numerous overlapping bands and identical signatures for different ionic species make speciation ambiguous. Quantum-chemical calculations are therefore used to connect spectral bands with solvation structures. Low-frequency extensions, including optical Kerr effect and broadband dielectric spectroscopy, probe collective motions, dipole/ionic relaxation, and diffusion, but their spectra can be difficult to model uniquely. Overall, spectroscopic speciation combines IR/Raman signatures, isotope editing, ultrafast methods, and computational calculations.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes spectroscopic speciation of a simulated aqueous electrolyte mixture containing five ionic species using simultaneous Raman and ATR-FTIR measurements. A three-step blind source-separation procedure was applied to identify spectral components and estimate relative species concentrations through one-point calibration. The number of sources was selected by inspecting singular values, leading to six components for both Raman and IR. The major analytical challenges were noise, weak or overlapping spectral features, and departures from linear Beer–Lambert behavior. In Raman spectra, phosphate was not recovered because its local signal-to-noise ratio was only about 10 dB, despite an average SNR of approximately 40 dB. Residuals also revealed deviations near nitrate and carbonate bands. A negative nitrate-associated peak together with a positive spurious source correlated with nitrate and nitrite was interpreted as evidence of nonlinear nitrate–nitrite interactions. Thus, nonlinear chemical or spectral interactions can generate misleading components and compromise straightforward concentration estimation. Under linear concentration dependence and linear spectral superposition, the blind procedure was effective for the IR data; under noise and mild nonlinearities, it still identified the principal species and produced molar-fraction estimates close to the actual values. Ion pairing is not explicitly discussed in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that molecular-level characterization of high-concentration electrolytes is challenging because increasing salt concentration lowers the static dielectric constant and strengthens electrostatic interactions, producing substantial ion association and larger, heterogeneous nanometric aggregates rather than only isolated solvated ions. These changes complicate interpretation of spectroscopic signals: spectral features may reflect overlapping populations of solvent-separated ion pairs, contact ion pairs, cation–anion and anion–anion pairs, hydrogen-bonded species, and n-AGGs. Consequently, ion pairing and collective aggregation can make spectral intensity or peak changes nonlinear with concentration, so spectra cannot necessarily be assigned using dilute-solution or independent-species assumptions. The approaches reported here combine spectroscopy with molecular dynamics rather than relying on spectroscopy alone. IR spectroscopy and MD simulations were used to identify substantial contact-ion-pair populations in concentrated LiTFSI aqueous electrolytes. FTIR together with MD was used to examine hydrogen bonding between water and anions and to assess proposed water-network structures. For the 21 m LiTFSI water-in-salt electrolyte, n-AGGs were investigated through a combination of MD simulations, neutron scattering, and spectroscopic techniques. These combined methods help distinguish local ion pairing from larger-scale aggregate structure and connect spectral observations with molecular models.
contexts.question: What are the challenges and approaches for characterizing high-concentration electrolytes at the molecular level using spectroscopy? How do ion pairing and nonlinear effects impact spectral analysis? What approaches have been used for spectroscopic speciation of concentrated electrolytes?

contexts.context: The excerpt compares conventional PLS, linear-quadratic PLS (LQ-PLS), quadratic PLS (QPLS), and artificial neural networks (ANNs) for nonlinear NIR calibration, but it does not discuss support-vector regression (SVR). Ordinary PLS is described as suitable for linear systems and for small deviations from linearity, while substantial nonlinearity from scattering or intrinsic absorption behavior can produce large prediction errors. SNV was identified as the best spectral pretreatment for reducing scattering-related nonlinearity; after SNV, PLS gave accurate results for a linear absorption band at 1450 nm. For intrinsically nonlinear systems, LQ-PLS, QPLS, and ANN reportedly produced comparable results. Overall, PC-ANN was identified as the best choice for the acrylic-fiber moisture application, although PLS or LQ-PLS combined with effective pretreatment achieved comparable performance with substantially less labor-intensive optimization. The passage explains that ANN training requires more training data than network weights and that PCA scores can be used as ANN inputs to reduce dimensionality, but it gives no exact number of calibration/training samples. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general methodological context for comparing PLS and ANN in spectroscopic calibration, but it does not report a specific NIR calibration experiment, training-set size, SVR model, or quantitative performance comparison. PLS is described as the most widely used chemometric calibration method. It projects spectral data onto latent variables selected to maximize covariance between predictor scores and responses, making the resulting components relevant to calibration. The number of latent variables is critical: too few can cause underfitting, while too many can cause overfitting and poor performance on new samples. Cross-validation is identified as an appropriate strategy for selecting the optimal number of latent variables and minimizing validation error. The text also notes that standard multivariate calibration generally assumes linear relationships, whereas nonlinear behavior can occur; artificial neural networks are presented as self-adaptive, massively parallel machine-learning models that can address such nonlinear relationships through training. No information is provided here about support vector regression (SVR), the amount of training data, specific validation design beyond the general mention of cross-validation, or key numerical differences among PLS, ANN, and SVR.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames PLSR (often called PLS) as a largely linear, lower-dimensional approach. It is widely accepted for NIR calibration and cell-culture monitoring because it is comparatively interpretable and fits regulatory lifecycle-management practices, but its predictive capacity can be limited when spectral relationships are nonlinear. ANN and SVR are presented as nonlinear alternatives with greater flexibility for modeling complex relationships. ANN uses supervised learning through weighted artificial neurons and biases to map spectra to concentrations. SVR maps inputs into a higher-dimensional feature space and fits a relatively flat regression function while constraining errors within an epsilon threshold; slack variables handle infeasible constraints. The cited literature generally reports ANNR and SVR as more predictive than PLSR for spectroscopic data, although this excerpt does not provide the study’s numerical performance results or establish which of ANN versus SVR was best. The study acquired 168 spectra from six CHO bioreactor cultures, using 135 samples for model calibration and 33 for validation. The calibration data were partitioned with the Kennard–Stone algorithm, and the validation set was withheld from calibration. Models predicted viable cell density, glucose, lactate, and glutamine from NIR spectra. A separate batch culture using ActiPro medium was also used as an independent test of prediction capability.
contexts.question: How do PLS, ANN, and SVR compare for NIR spectroscopy calibration in nonlinear systems? How much training data was used, how were models validated, and what were the key performance differences?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a controlled comparison of PLSR, artificial neural-network regression (ANNR), and support-vector regression (SVR) for monitoring CHO-cell cultures with in situ NIR spectra, including compounds exhibiting nonlinear behavior. The main dataset contained 168 samples: 135 calibration samples used for model development and cross-validation, and 33 independent validation samples reserved for final performance assessment. Samples were partitioned with the Kennard–Stone algorithm, and the validation set was not used during calibration. PLSR latent-variable selection used venetian-windows cross-validation based on Q²Y. The same selected spectral preprocessing was applied across methods to make the regression comparison fair. SVR used an epsilon-regression formulation with a Gaussian radial-basis kernel, with gamma and epsilon optimized by venetian-windows cross-validation. ANNR architecture was screened for neuron number, and early stopping with tanh activation was used to limit overfitting. Models were selected using low RMSECV and RMSEP. Quantitative comparison was defined around accuracy (RMSEP), precision (mean residual and residual-variance tests), and linearity (calibration R² and Durbin–Watson analysis). Qualitative validation used repeated real-time spectra, including inter-batch heterogeneity, glucose-spiking specificity, internal validation, and an independent culture medium for external validation. However, these pages do not report the actual method-by-method performance differences; they only establish the design and validation framework. PCA indicated nonlinear concentration–spectral relationships particularly for ammonium and glutamine, while VCD and glucose were more linear over much of their ranges.
contexts.question: How do PLS, ANN, and SVR compare for NIR spectroscopy calibration in nonlinear systems? How much training data was used, how were models validated, and what were the key performance differences?

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that NIR calibration relationships in CHO cell cultures were nonlinear, limiting conventional PLSR. PLSR was vulnerable to inter-batch heterogeneity, extrapolation, and lack of analyte specificity: it often followed overall culture progression rather than glucose-specific spectral information and could predict the wrong direction after glucose spiking. SVR and ANN regression were introduced to address nonlinear behavior. SVR’s sample-based, nonlinear approach could identify unusual calibration samples and performed especially well for glucose under spiking conditions and for viable-cell prediction. However, SVR showed a substantial offset and weaker performance during the initial part of one robustness experiment. ANN performed well for glutamine, had less prediction bounce than PLSR for ammonium, and generalized glucose behavior better across major culture-medium variations; the authors therefore regarded ANN as potentially preferable when large media changes are expected. All methods struggled with some abrupt changes and late-culture lactate predictions, although PLSR and ANN generally showed more bounce than SVR. This excerpt does not state the total amount of training data, the exact calibration/training split, or the formal validation procedure. It does note that glucose-spiked samples formed only a negligible fraction of the ANN calibration set, affecting generalization, and that robustness was evaluated empirically using additional culture conditions.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that PLSR was limited for NIR calibration when spectra–concentration relationships were nonlinear, as observed for several cell-culture analytes. Nonlinearity was especially pronounced at process extremes and for lactate, mAb, ammonium, and glutamine; therefore, nonlinear methods were used: SVR as a sample-based method and ANN/ANNR as a variable-based method. Across all compounds, SVR and ANNR produced lower RMSEP values than PLSR, although the differences were not statistically significant by one-way ANOVA with Tukey testing because confidence intervals overlapped. For glucose, RMSEP values were 3.37 mM for PLSR, 2.29 mM for SVR, and 1.32 mM for ANNR. Residual-variance analysis with Levene’s test suggested that SVR and ANNR were more precise than PLSR, with SVR generally outperforming ANNR; for viable-cell density, precision values were 3.28, 0.25, and 0.54 ×10^5 cells/mL for PLSR, SVR, and ANNR, respectively. SVR and ANNR also generally improved R² and residual linearity, though ANNR remained problematic for glutamine and lactate. This excerpt does not specify the amount of training data, train/test split, or complete validation design; it only reports calibration-model comparisons and statistical analyses.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames PLSR as the conventional calibration method for CHO-cell-culture NIR monitoring, but emphasizes that it maps spectra linearly and cannot natively represent nonlinear relationships between spectra and analyte concentrations. Such nonlinearities arise from complex aqueous media, scattering, noisy spectra, confused compound relationships, inter-batch heterogeneity, and process changes. ANN regression (ANNR) and support-vector regression (SVR) were evaluated as nonlinear alternatives and are reported to handle these complications better, with improved specificity and inter-batch robustness. For glucose, the abstract gives determination coefficients of 0.85 for PLSR, 0.93 for SVR, and 0.98 for ANNR, indicating the strongest performance for ANNR and intermediate performance for SVR. The excerpt states that SVR and ANNR improve the potential of NIR spectroscopy for real-time monitoring. However, the supplied pages do not report how much training data was used, the precise calibration/training split, cross-validation or external-validation procedure, or the full performance results for all monitored parameters. They only note that appropriate validation should address accuracy, precision, specificity, linearity, operating range, robustness, and lifecycle management. Thus, the nonlinear-model performance comparison is supported, but the requested dataset size and detailed validation methodology require later sections of the article.
contexts.question: How do PLS, ANN, and SVR compare for NIR spectroscopy calibration in nonlinear systems? How much training data was used, how were models validated, and what were the key performance differences?

contexts.context: The excerpt compares PLS regression (PLSR), artificial neural-network regression (ANNR), and support-vector regression (SVR) for nonlinear NIR calibration of CHO-cell culture analytes. Although high R² values did not necessarily ensure linear agreement between predicted and actual concentrations, nonlinear SVR and ANNR generally reduced residual correlation and produced more linear predictions than PLSR. SVR was described as the most accurate and precise method overall, while ANNR did not achieve linear prediction for some compounds, particularly glutamine and lactate. During real-time monitoring, PLSR was especially vulnerable to inter-batch heterogeneity: batch-specific trajectories that differed from the calibration trajectory caused offsets and mispredictions. SVR and ANNR improved glucose predictions, particularly at the beginning of cultures and for a strongly deviating batch, although heterogeneity still affected both methods late in the process. In a glucose-spiking specificity test, SVR correctly tracked an increase to approximately 20 mM, whereas ANNR and PLSR predicted only about 16 and 7 mM, respectively; PLSR and ANNR also incorrectly predicted a later glucose increase. The excerpt describes calibration and qualitative evaluation across multiple batches, PCA trajectory analysis, offline reference comparisons, and an independent glucose-spiking test, but it does not specify the amount of training data, exact train/validation split, cross-validation procedure, or numerical performance metrics.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: State of the art in coupling IN-LINE / IN-SITU VIBRATIONAL SPECTROSCOPY (ATR-FTIR, Raman, NIR, UV-Vis) to automated liquid-handling or flow systems as a real-time composition sensor, and in SENSOR FUSION where spectroscopy is measured SIMULTANEOUSLY with a physical property such as ionic conductivity on the same sample. Cite specific papers with DOIs. Cover: (a) combined ATR-FTIR + conductivity flow cells for electrolyte speciation; (b) chemometrics (PLS, MCR-ALS, classical least squares) versus neural-network / nonlinear models for predicting concentrations of all species from a spectrum of a concentrated multicomponent electrolyte where ion pairing makes the spectral mixing NONLINEAR and Beer-Lambert additivity fails; (c) how much training data those models needed and how they were validated on held-out or blind test sets; (d) Raman versus IR practicality for fiber-coupled integration into a robot.

# State of the Art: In-Line Vibrational Spectroscopy Coupled to Automated/Flow Systems and Sensor Fusion for Electrolyte Composition Monitoring

## Overview

The coupling of vibrational spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR, Raman, NIR, UV-Vis) with automated liquid-handling or flow systems as real-time composition sensors has advanced substantially, driven by process analytical technology (PAT) frameworks and the emerging self-driving laboratory paradigm. Simultaneously, sensor fusion — the combination of spectroscopy with physical property measurements such as ionic conductivity on the same sample — has been demonstrated in several application domains. The following synthesizes the current literature across the four requested areas.

The table below summarizes the key studies discussed in this review.

| Reference | Spectroscopy modality | Physical property co-measured | System type | Chemometric method | Training-data size | Validation approach | Key findings |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bryan, Levitskaia & Casella (2013), conference paper; DOI not reported | Fiber-coupled Raman + Vis–NIR | Conductivity, Coriolis density, temperature and flow | Nuclear-reprocessing flow loop / centrifugal contactor | PLS models trained on static spectra | Not reported | Applied to online centrifugal-contactor extraction tests | Demonstrated multimodal process monitoring: Raman quantified concentrated Raman-active species, Vis–NIR addressed actinides/lanthanides, and conductivity/density added independent bulk-composition constraints. (bryan2013spectroscopiconlinemonitoring pages 1-3) |
| Kachko et al. (2015), DOI: [10.1021/acs.iecr.5b00691](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.5b00691) | Fiber-coupled NIR absorption | Conductivity, density, pH, sound velocity, refractive index and temperature | Flow-through bypass on a CO₂-capture pilot plant; approximately 850 h online | Temperature-dependent PLS; 3 latent variables for AMP and 2 each for PZ and CO₂ | 53 designed compositions initially; 12 precipitating samples excluded; reported design included 27 training and 26 testing compositions | Leave-one-out cross-validation for latent-variable selection; pilot predictions compared with offline LC–MS for AMP/PZ and hot-phosphoric-acid CO₂ analysis | Predicted AMP, PZ and CO₂ with average pilot/offline deviations of ±1.8%, ±1.3% and ±3.9%. This is strong evidence for spectroscopy–conductivity sensor fusion, but it used NIR—not ATR-FTIR.
